body:
Why Coastal Areas Need Special Protection

A coast is the meeting place of land and sea. It contains beaches, sand dunes, estuaries, mangroves, mudflats, coral reefs and other ecosystems. These environments are continuously influenced by tides, waves, sediment movement and, in many places, river water.

Coastal areas are ecologically important and economically valuable. Mangroves provide habitat for aquatic organisms, support fisheries and help reduce the impact of waves and storm surges. Sand dunes act as natural barriers against coastal erosion and flooding. Estuaries, where river water mixes with seawater, provide productive habitats for fish and other organisms. Coral reefs support marine biodiversity and can reduce wave energy.

At the same time, coasts are used for fishing, ports, shipping, tourism, industries, settlements and transport infrastructure. Unregulated construction, destruction of mangroves, sand mining, untreated wastewater and obstruction of natural tidal flows can damage coastal ecosystems and increase disaster risks.

Coastal regulation therefore aims to conserve sensitive environments while allowing specified economic activities and protecting the livelihoods of coastal communities. It is a system of regulated development, not a declaration that every human activity near the sea is prohibited.

Legal Basis of the Coastal Regulation Zone

The Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) is the coastal land and water area in which specified activities are restricted, prohibited or permitted subject to conditions under notifications issued using the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.

The Central Government, through the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC), regulates these areas under Section 3 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. The principal stages of India's CRZ framework are:

  • 19 February 1991: The first CRZ Notification established a framework for regulating activities along the coast.
  • 6 January 2011: A revised notification provided a more detailed classification and strengthened provisions concerning coastal communities and sensitive environments.
  • 18 January 2019: CRZ Notification, 2019, issued as G.S.R. 37(E), introduced revised categories, population-based rural regulation and updated clearance provisions. It has subsequently been amended.

The 2019 Rules Do Not Apply Everywhere Automatically

The revised 2019 provisions become operational for a coastal area when its Coastal Zone Management Plan (CZMP) has been updated and approved under the 2019 notification. Until that happens, the applicable provisions of the 2011 framework continue to govern that area. This distinction is essential when applying the 50 m and 200 m rules.

Understanding the High Tide Line and Low Tide Line

The High Tide Line (HTL) is the line on land up to which the highest water level reaches during spring tide, as officially demarcated under the notification. It is not simply the point where a wave reaches on a particular day. The National Centre for Sustainable Coastal Management (NCSCM), Chennai, has a specified role in demarcating the HTL, the Low Tide Line and ecologically sensitive areas.

The Low Tide Line (LTL) marks the corresponding low-water boundary. The land between the HTL and LTL is called the intertidal zone. It may be submerged at high tide and exposed at low tide.

How Far Does the CRZ Extend?

  • Along the open sea: Generally, the land extending 500 m landward from the HTL is included.
  • Between HTL and LTL: The intertidal land is included.
  • Into the sea: The water and seabed from the LTL to the territorial-water limit of 12 nautical miles are included.
  • Along tidal rivers, creeks, estuaries and backwaters: The 2019 framework regulates land up to 50 m from the HTL or the width of the creek or water body, whichever is less, after approval of the revised CZMP. Until then, the earlier 100 m or water-body-width limit continues.

The inland extent of tidal influence is determined using a salinity concentration of 5 parts per thousand during the driest season. This prevents the CRZ boundary from being extended indefinitely along an ordinary freshwater river.

The mainland CRZ Notification, 2019, does not directly govern the Andaman and Nicobar or Lakshadweep island groups. These have a separate Island Coastal Regulation Zone framework.

Prelims focus

  • CRZ regulations are issued under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
  • The first CRZ Notification was issued on 19 February 1991; major revised notifications followed in 2011 and 2019.
  • The general seafront landward extent is 500 m from the HTL.
  • The seaward extent reaches 12 nautical miles from the LTL.
  • Tidal influence is identified using salinity of 5 parts per thousand in the driest season.
  • Trap: Publication of the 2019 notification alone does not establish that its revised limits apply to every coastal district.

[Sources: MoEFCC, Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, 2019, G.S.R. 37(E), preamble and paragraphs 1-2, dated 18 January 2019; MoEFCC, Annual Report 2025-26, Environmental Impact Assessment and Clearance, pp. 54-56; NCERT, Class 12 Biology, Chapter 15, Biodiversity and Conservation; NCERT, Class 11 Indian Economic Development, Chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development; consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: India's coastal ecosystems support biodiversity, livelihoods and protection from natural hazards.

title: Coastal Regulation Zone: Purpose, Legal Basis and Geographical Extent

body:
Why the Coast Is Divided into Different Zones

Different coastal locations have different ecological conditions and patterns of settlement. A mangrove forest cannot be regulated in the same way as an already developed urban waterfront. Similarly, fishing activities in coastal waters differ from construction on rural coastal land.

The CRZ Notification, 2019, therefore classifies regulated areas primarily by ecological sensitivity, level of development, population density and whether the area is land or water.

CategoryArea coveredMain distinguishing feature
CRZ-IAEcologically sensitive coastal areasMangroves, coral reefs, sand dunes, biologically active mudflats and other protected features
CRZ-IBLand between LTL and HTLIntertidal zone
CRZ-IISubstantially developed urban coastal landSpecified urban limits, more than 50% built-up plots and supporting infrastructure
CRZ-IIIADensely populated CRZ-III landPopulation density above 2161 persons per sq km under Census 2011
CRZ-IIIBOther less densely populated CRZ-III landPopulation density below 2161 persons per sq km under Census 2011
CRZ-IVASea water and seabedFrom LTL to 12 nautical miles seaward
CRZ-IVBTidal rivers, creeks and similar watersWater and bed between the opposite LTLs up to the defined tidal limit

CRZ-I: Ecologically Most Sensitive Areas

CRZ-IA

CRZ-IA includes ecologically sensitive areas and coastal landforms that help maintain the integrity of the coast. Important examples are mangroves, corals and coral reefs, sand dunes, biologically active mudflats, salt marshes, seagrass beds, turtle nesting grounds, bird nesting areas, specified protected areas and certain heritage sites.

These areas require strict protection because even a small physical alteration can affect habitats, tidal movement or coastal stability. The notification also provides for a 50 m buffer around mangrove areas exceeding 1000 sq m on government land, subject to the detailed conditions in its ecological management provisions. Mangroves on private land remain protected, but the notification's management provisions do not require the same external buffer on private mangrove land. Land declared as forest also attracts the applicable forest law.

CRZ-IB

CRZ-IB is the intertidal strip between the LTL and HTL. It can include sandy beaches and tidal surfaces. It is not defined by the presence of mangroves or coral reefs. Some foreshore-dependent activities may be regulated and permitted here, but unrestricted construction is not allowed.

CRZ-II: Already Developed Urban Coastal Areas

CRZ-II applies to coastal land within existing municipal limits or other legally designated urban areas that are substantially built up. Under the 2019 definition, the ratio of built-up plots to total plots must exceed 50%, and drainage, approach roads and other infrastructural facilities, such as water supply or sewerage, must exist.

Construction and reconstruction may be permitted subject to conditions, including the general requirement that new buildings be situated on the landward side of an existing road or an existing authorised structure, together with applicable planning and building rules. The aim is to accommodate already developed settlements without allowing unrestricted expansion towards the sea.

A site does not become CRZ-II merely because it is near a town or falls inside municipal limits. The notification's development and infrastructure criteria must also be satisfied.

CRZ-III: Relatively Undisturbed and Other Coastal Land

CRZ-III consists of relatively undisturbed areas, commonly rural coastal stretches, and other coastal land not qualifying as CRZ-II. The 2019 framework separates it into CRZ-IIIA and CRZ-IIIB using Census 2011 population density.

The most important difference is the width of the No Development Zone (NDZ): ordinarily 50 m in CRZ-IIIA once the revised CZMP is approved, compared with 200 m in CRZ-IIIB. The conditions governing this distinction are examined separately.

CRZ-IV: Coastal Water Areas

CRZ-IVA consists of sea water and seabed from the LTL to 12 nautical miles. CRZ-IVB covers water and the bed of tidal-influenced water bodies, such as creeks and estuaries, between their opposite low-tide boundaries. Its inland extent reaches the legally identified tidal limit, associated with salinity of 5 parts per thousand in the driest season.

Traditional fishing and allied activities are recognised in CRZ-IV. Other projects, including foreshore facilities, remain subject to the applicable restrictions and permissions.

Prelims focus

  • CRZ-IA means ecologically sensitive areas; CRZ-IB means intertidal land.
  • CRZ-II requires substantially developed urban land with more than 50% built-up plots and specified infrastructure.
  • CRZ-IIIA and CRZ-IIIB are subdivisions of CRZ-III based on Census 2011 density.
  • CRZ-IVA covers marine water up to 12 nautical miles; CRZ-IVB covers tidal-influenced inland water bodies.
  • Trap: CRZ-IB is not the same as CRZ-IVB. The former is intertidal land; the latter is tidal water and its bed.

[Sources: MoEFCC, Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, 2019, paragraph 2 and Annexure I, dated 18 January 2019, with subsequent amendments; MoEFCC, Standard Operating Procedure for Authorised Agencies for Preparation of CRZ Maps, Section 5.2, October 2023; NCERT, Class 12 Biology, Chapter 15, Biodiversity and Conservation; consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A decision tree classifies sensitive areas, intertidal land, developed and other coastal land, and coastal waters into CRZ categories.
pictures.caption: CRZ classification first distinguishes sensitive habitats, developed land, other land and water areas.

title: Classification of Coastal Regulation Zones: CRZ-I, II, III and IV

body:
Meaning of a No Development Zone

A No Development Zone (NDZ) is a specified coastal strip within which ordinary new construction is restricted, while particular activities expressly allowed by the CRZ notification may continue subject to conditions.

The expression does not mean that people must leave the area or that farming and fishing automatically become illegal. It means that development rights are restricted to safeguard the shoreline, coastal ecosystems and local communities.

CRZ-IIIA and CRZ-IIIB Under the 2019 Framework

The population criterion for the 2019 rural classification is based on Census 2011, not a later estimate of a village's population. The applicable NDZ also depends on whether the revised CZMP has been approved.

ConditionClassificationSeafront NDZ
Density above 2161 persons per sq km; approved 2019 CZMPCRZ-IIIA50 m from HTL
Density above 2161 persons per sq km; revised CZMP not approvedCRZ-IIIA under proposed classification200 m continues
Density below 2161 persons per sq kmCRZ-IIIB200 m from HTL

The reduction from 200 m to 50 m for densely populated CRZ-IIIA stretches recognises settlement pressure, but it is conditional. A proposed 2019 map is not equivalent to an approved 2019 CZMP.

The Special Rule Along Tidal Water Bodies

In CRZ-III areas adjoining tidal-influenced rivers, creeks and similar waters, the 2019 framework identifies an NDZ of 50 m or the width of the water body, whichever is less, after approval of the revised CZMP. The previous corresponding limit is 100 m or the width of the water body, whichever is less, until the updated plan becomes applicable.

For example, if the relevant creek is 30 m wide, the landward regulatory distance under the 2019 rule is limited to 30 m rather than 50 m. This is a conceptual illustration; actual boundaries must be checked against the approved official map.

The notification provides that the CRZ-III NDZ restriction does not apply within notified port limits. This does not remove other CRZ restrictions, environmental-clearance requirements or conditions applicable to ports.

What Is Permitted Within an NDZ?

Paragraph 5.3 of the 2019 notification identifies activities that may be permitted or regulated within CRZ-III NDZ areas. Important examples include:

  • Existing authorised buildings: Repairs or reconstruction without exceeding the existing permitted floor-space index, plinth area and density, subject to applicable conditions.
  • Traditional coastal communities: Specified construction or reconstruction of dwellings associated with traditional coastal communities, including fishers, with provisions for sanitation and disaster safety.
  • Land-based activities: Agriculture, horticulture, gardens, pastures, parks, playfields and forestry.
  • Fishing-related facilities: Fish-drying yards, net-mending yards, auction halls, traditional boat-building yards and specified fish-handling facilities.
  • Essential community infrastructure: Schools, dispensaries, community toilets, public shelters, water supply, drainage, roads, bridges and electric substations when permitted on a case-by-case basis by the competent Coastal Zone Management Authority.
  • Limited tourism facilities: Temporary facilities such as approved shacks, toilets and walkways, subject to the approved tourism plan, safeguards and specified setbacks.

Temporary tourism facilities permitted under the relevant provision must maintain a minimum distance of 10 m from HTL. The exception is not a general licence for permanent hotels within the NDZ.

Development Beyond the NDZ

Being outside the NDZ does not mean being outside the CRZ. For example, land 300 m from the HTL may lie beyond a 200 m NDZ but still be within the general 500 m coastal regulatory extent.

In eligible CRZ-III areas beyond the NDZ, certain dwelling units, public infrastructure and tourism projects may be permitted under specified conditions. For dwelling construction under the provision concerning traditional rights and customary use, the notification specifies a maximum building height of 9 m and 2 floors, consisting of ground and 1 upper floor, in addition to applicable local planning rules.

NDZ width and CRZ extent are different measurements. The NDZ restricts a narrower strip; the wider CRZ continues to regulate activities beyond that strip.

Prelims focus

  • CRZ-IIIA uses Census 2011 density above 2161 persons per sq km.
  • Its 50 m NDZ requires an approved CZMP under the 2019 notification.
  • CRZ-IIIB generally retains a 200 m seafront NDZ.
  • The revised tidal-creek limit is 50 m or water-body width, whichever is less.
  • Specified temporary tourism facilities must maintain at least 10 m from the HTL.
  • Trap: An NDZ does not prohibit every traditional livelihood activity or authorised repair.

[Sources: MoEFCC, Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, 2019, paragraphs 2.3 and 5.3, and Annexure III; MoEFCC, Standard Operating Procedure for Authorised Agencies for Preparation of CRZ Maps, Section 5.2, October 2023; MoEFCC, Annual Report 2025-26, Environmental Impact Assessment and Clearance, pp. 54-56; consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: CRZ-IIIA gets a 50 m NDZ only with approved 2019 mapping; otherwise 200 m continues. CRZ-IIIB has 200 m. General CRZ extent stays 500 m.
pictures.caption: The 50 m rule for CRZ-IIIA depends on both population density and approved mapping.

title: No Development Zones, Population Density and Construction Restrictions

body:
Why Coastal Activities Are Regulated Differently

A port, fishing jetty, road, hotel, industrial plant and sewage outlet have different effects on coastal land and water. Some activities must be located near the shore to function, while others can operate farther inland. CRZ regulation distinguishes between these needs and the environmental risks created.

The notification establishes general prohibitions and then provides specific exceptions and regulated permissions for different zones. Therefore, deciding whether an activity can take place requires reading the prohibition and the relevant exception together.

Activities Generally Prohibited in CRZ Areas

Paragraph 4 of CRZ Notification, 2019, generally prohibits the following activities, subject to the exceptions expressly provided elsewhere in the notification:

  • Establishing new industries or expanding existing industrial operations and processes.
  • Manufacturing or handling specified hazardous substances, including specified oil-related activities, except as permitted under particular provisions.
  • Establishing new fish-processing units.
  • Undertaking unauthorised land reclamation, bunding or alteration of the natural course of seawater.
  • Discharging untreated waste or effluents from industries, settlements, cities or towns.
  • Dumping municipal waste, construction debris, industrial solid waste or fly ash for land filling.
  • Undertaking port and harbour projects in stretches identified as highly eroding coasts.
  • Mining sand, rocks and other underlying materials, except where specifically permitted.
  • Altering active sand dunes or disposing of plastic into coastal waters.
  • Drawing groundwater where prohibited by the relevant zone-specific provisions.

General Prohibition Does Not Mean There Are No Exceptions

The law provides narrowly defined exceptions for some activities. For example, a regulated port facility may be allowed even though new industries and reclamation are generally prohibited. The exception must be established from the correct paragraph and approved by the competent authority; it cannot be assumed merely because the project serves an economic purpose.

Activities That May Be Permitted with Conditions

Foreshore-Dependent Infrastructure

Foreshore-dependent activities are activities that directly require access to the sea or shoreline. Examples include ports, harbours, jetties, wharves, navigation facilities, certain pipelines, seawater-intake arrangements and specified erosion-control structures. These may be allowed under the relevant CRZ provisions with prior permission and safeguards.

The necessity of a coastal location is important. A general office building or unrelated factory does not become foreshore-dependent simply because its owner prefers a sea-facing site.

Traditional Fishing and Related Facilities

Traditional fishing and allied activities are expressly recognised in CRZ-IV. In appropriate land categories, facilities for net repair, fish drying, boat building and fish landing may be permitted. Such activities support the existing economic life of coastal communities.

There is an important distinction between a traditional fish-drying yard or other permitted fishing facility and a new industrial fish-processing unit, which falls under the general prohibition. They are not legally identical merely because both concern fish.

Tourism and Reconstruction

Hotels and resorts are not freely permitted throughout the CRZ. Their location, permitted building characteristics and environmental safeguards depend on the zone and applicable tourism plan. In some beach or NDZ areas, carefully regulated temporary tourism facilities may be permitted even where ordinary permanent buildings are restricted.

Reconstruction is also different from construction of an entirely new building. An existing authorised structure may be eligible for repair or reconstruction within limits that would not permit an unrelated new project.

Environmental Effects of Inappropriate Coastal Development

Removing mangroves for construction can destroy fish habitats and reduce natural protection from storm surges. Altering dunes and beaches can increase erosion. Reclamation can change tidal flow and sediment transport. Untreated sewage may introduce harmful organisms and nutrients into estuaries, affecting water quality and aquatic life.

These connections explain why a project may need to demonstrate not only that it falls into a permitted category but also that its design, location and operation will protect coastal processes and nearby communities.

Applying the Rules to Simple Examples

Example 1: A fishing cooperative proposes a net-mending yard in a CRZ-III fishing village. The activity is specifically recognised among facilities for local fishing communities, so it may be considered subject to applicable conditions.

Example 2: A developer proposes filling a tidal mudflat to construct an ordinary commercial complex. Reclamation is generally prohibited, and an ecologically sensitive mudflat may fall within CRZ-IA. The project cannot be justified merely by claiming that it creates employment.

Example 3: A public agency proposes a stand-alone jetty. The activity may be permitted under the relevant provisions, but its classification, environmental effects and competent clearance authority must still be established.

Prelims focus

  • Untreated effluent discharge is prohibited in CRZ areas.
  • Unauthorised reclamation, harmful sand mining and destruction of active dunes are generally prohibited.
  • Traditional fishing and specified fishing facilities are recognised under the notification.
  • Ports, jetties and erosion-control works can be regulated activities rather than automatically prohibited activities.
  • Trap: The legal treatment of an activity depends on both the general prohibition and the applicable zone-specific exception.

[Sources: MoEFCC, Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, 2019, paragraphs 4-5 and Annexures I and III; MoEFCC, amendment S.O. 5495(E), dated 24 November 2022; NCERT, Class 12 Biology, Chapter 15, Biodiversity and Conservation, and Chapter 16, Environmental Issues; consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Engineers inspect a jetty as workers carry materials beside an Indian harbour, with fishing boats nearby and an intact natural shore beyond.
pictures.caption: Coastal development must be assessed alongside sensitive habitats and existing livelihoods.

pictures.alt: Causal arrows connect coastal alterations to habitat loss, weaker storm protection, erosion, changed coastal flows, water pollution and fishing livelihood impacts.

title: Prohibited and Permitted Coastal Activities: Applying CRZ Rules

body:
Why a Coastal Map Has Legal Importance

A regulation referring to a distance from the High Tide Line cannot be implemented reliably unless the relevant boundary is identified on an official map. Similarly, the designation of mangroves, coral areas, dunes and other sensitive habitats affects the activities that can be permitted on a particular plot.

A Coastal Zone Management Plan (CZMP) is an officially prepared and approved planning document that identifies the applicable coastal boundaries, CRZ categories, ecologically sensitive areas and other regulated coastal features for the relevant area.

Under the 2019 framework, states and Union territories prepare or update their plans through authorised agencies and prescribed consultation procedures. The concerned CZMA holds district-level public hearings on draft plans, which are revised in light of suggestions and objections before MoEFCC approval. Once approved, they guide the authorities deciding individual project proposals.

What Is Shown on a CZMP?

Important information includes:

  • The officially demarcated HTL and LTL.
  • CRZ-IA, CRZ-IB, CRZ-II, CRZ-III and CRZ-IV boundaries, including relevant subdivisions.
  • Mangroves, coral reefs, sand dunes, ecologically sensitive areas and their applicable buffers.
  • The extent of tidal influence along creeks, rivers and estuaries.
  • Important settlements, infrastructure and other features needed for coastal planning.
  • Relevant No Development Zone boundaries and permitted-use conditions.

The CZMP framework uses maps at a scale of 1:25,000. For an individual project seeking clearance, the notification's procedure also requires an appropriate site-specific CRZ map at 1:4000, prepared by an authorised agency using the applicable officially demarcated boundaries. The more detailed map helps authorities assess the precise location of proposed works.

A CZMP classifies and regulates land and water. It does not itself grant permission to every project appearing within a zone. A project may still require separate clearance.

Authorities Involved in Coastal Regulation

InstitutionMain function
MoEFCCIssues central CRZ regulations, approves updated plans and grants specified clearances.
National Coastal Zone Management AuthorityCoordinates State and Union Territory CZMAs and reviews proposed changes to CRZ classifications and CZMPs.
State or Union Territory Coastal Zone Management AuthorityReviews coastal proposals, makes recommendations, grants specified clearances and supports enforcement.
NCSCM, ChennaiProvides specified scientific coastal demarcation and mapping inputs.
SEIAAGrants environmental clearance for Category B projects covered by the EIA Notification, 2006, following the applicable appraisal process.

Which Authority Grants the Clearance?

The deciding authority depends on the project's location and whether it also attracts environmental clearance under the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Notification, 2006. An EIA examines likely environmental effects before a decision is taken, including impacts that may require avoidance, mitigation or monitoring.

The important clearance distinctions under the 2019 notification, as amended on 24 November 2022, are:

  • Projects also requiring EIA clearance: The Coastal Zone Management Authority forwards its recommendation so that Category A projects are considered by the Central Government and Category B projects by the State Environment Impact Assessment Authority, as applicable, through the composite clearance procedure.
  • Projects outside the EIA Notification but requiring CRZ clearance in CRZ-I or CRZ-IV: These are generally considered by the Central Government on the recommendation of the concerned Coastal Zone Management Authority.
  • Specified exceptions in CRZ-I and CRZ-IV: Stand-alone jetties, salt works, slipways, temporary structures and specified erosion-control measures are assigned to the concerned Coastal Zone Management Authority under the 2022 amendment.
  • Projects outside the EIA Notification but requiring CRZ clearance solely in CRZ-II or CRZ-III: These are generally considered by the concerned Coastal Zone Management Authority.

Where a proposal crosses different CRZ categories, the complete location and the relevant special provisions must be considered. A project cannot avoid stricter scrutiny by describing only its least sensitive component.

How a Coastal Proposal Is Examined

  1. Establish the location: Determine the applicable approved CZMP, officially demarcated HTL and LTL, and the CRZ category.
  2. Identify the activity: Check whether the proposed work is prohibited, permitted or permitted only subject to conditions.
  3. Prepare the required documents: These may include the site-specific CRZ map, project details and environmental studies where applicable.
  4. Obtain the CZMA's consideration or recommendation: The authority examines the proposal against the regulation and approved map.
  5. Obtain the required decision: The competent central, state-level or coastal-zone authority grants or refuses clearance under the applicable procedure.
  6. Comply with conditions: A clearance may impose limits, environmental safeguards and monitoring duties. Other statutory permissions may also be needed.

Public consultation and hearings are important in the preparation of revised CZMPs and may also form part of environmental appraisal where required. Coastal fishers and other affected communities can provide information about customary access, fishing grounds and local environmental risks.

Prelims focus

  • CZMP is the approved coastal planning and classification document.
  • The CZMP mapping scale is 1:25,000; project-specific CRZ mapping uses 1:4000.
  • NCSCM, Chennai, performs the specified scientific demarcation role.
  • For projects also covered by EIA Notification, 2006, Category A and Category B follow different competent-authority routes.
  • The 2022 amendment delegates specified small coastal infrastructure clearances, including stand-alone jetties, to the concerned CZMA.
  • Trap: A project may be permissible in principle without having received the clearance required to begin work.

[Sources: MoEFCC, Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, 2019, paragraphs 6-8 and guidelines for preparation of CZMPs; MoEFCC, S.O. 5495(E), amendment dated 24 November 2022, amendments to paragraphs 7-8; MoEFCC, Standard Operating Procedure for Authorised Agencies for Preparation of CRZ Maps, October 2023; consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A decision flow uses the approved CZMP, EIA applicability and CRZ category to identify Central Government, SEIAA or CZMA as the final authority.
pictures.caption: CRZ clearance depends on both the mapped zone and whether the project also requires EIA clearance.

title: Coastal Zone Management Plans, Mapping and Environmental Clearances

body:
Why Gujarat Is Important for Coastal Environmental Governance

Gujarat has extensive coastal areas along the Arabian Sea, including the Gulf of Kachchh and the Gulf of Khambhat. These coastal regions contain important tidal habitats and support fishing, shipping, ports, salt production, industry and coastal settlements.

The environmental challenge is not limited to conserving individual species. Coastal authorities must also consider tidal exchange, sediment movement, mangroves, intertidal mudflats, marine habitats, fishing access and risks from industrial or infrastructure projects.

Critically Vulnerable Coastal Areas

Critically Vulnerable Coastal Areas (CVCAs) are specially identified coastal areas requiring particular attention to ecological protection and the needs of communities dependent on coastal resources.

Paragraph 3.1 of CRZ Notification, 2019, specifically identifies the Gulf of Kachchh and Gulf of Khambhat among the important coastal areas requiring special consideration. Other examples listed in the notification include the Sundarban region, Gulf of Mannar and Bhitarkanika.

These areas are to be managed with the involvement of coastal communities, including fishing communities. The notification provides for Integrated Management Plans (IMPs) that consider environmental conservation as well as local requirements such as access, schools, shelters, water supply, drainage, roads and jetties.

This approach recognises that conservation and livelihood protection must be considered together. It does not mean that every activity throughout an entire gulf is automatically banned. The precise controls arise from the applicable notifications, mapped categories and approved plans.

Development and Livelihood Conflicts

Consider a proposed coastal project involving a jetty, access road or industrial water-intake facility. The project may provide employment and transport benefits, but it can also affect coastal ecosystems and local livelihoods if poorly located or operated.

Development issuePossible environmental or social effectRelevant regulatory consideration
Reclamation near a mudflatLoss of habitat and altered tidal flowCRZ classification and reclamation restrictions
Jetty near fishing settlementsChanges to boat access or fishing activityForeshore permission and community needs
Industry near a creekRisk of effluent pollution and habitat damageCRZ restrictions, pollution controls and clearance
Construction near mangrovesLoss of ecological protection and nursery habitatCRZ-IA mapping and ecological safeguards

The appropriate decision may involve refusing an unsuitable activity, changing its location or design, imposing safeguards, or permitting specified traditional community facilities. Permission must arise from the legal provisions, not from a general claim that development is necessary.

Status of Revised CZMPs in Gujarat

The implementation status of CRZ Notification, 2019, is a changing administrative fact. It must be tied to an identifiable official report rather than treated as a permanent geographical fact.

In its Annual Report 2025-26, MoEFCC reported approval of updated CZMPs under the 2019 notification for 8 Gujarat districts: Vadodara, Anand, Ahmedabad, Porbandar, Junagadh, Dev Bhumi Dwarka, Jamnagar and Gir Somnath.

The report's stated progress period is 1 January 2025 to 31 December 2025. This is the period to which the reported approval position belongs. It should not be interpreted as a guarantee that the same list remained exhaustive after that period.

For an actual site in Gujarat, the applicable legally approved CZMP and subsequent official approvals determine whether the 2019 or transitional provisions govern. A recommendation to approve a plan must not be confused with final approval.

Gujarat and the National Green Tribunal

Where a substantial environmental dispute arising under an Act in Schedule I of the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, concerns Gujarat, the Western Zone Bench at Pune is the relevant zonal bench under the Tribunal's territorial allocation. The Gujarat Coastal Zone Management Authority deals with its regulatory responsibilities; the NGT exercises its separate adjudicatory and appellate powers.

Prelims focus

  • The Gulf of Kachchh and Gulf of Khambhat are specifically identified under the CVCA provisions of CRZ Notification, 2019.
  • CVCAs require attention to both ecological conservation and the livelihoods of coastal communities.
  • Integrated Management Plans are provided for CVCAs.
  • MoEFCC's Annual Report 2025-26 reported approved 2019 CZMPs for 8 named Gujarat districts during the period ending 31 December 2025.
  • Gujarat falls under the NGT's Western Zone Bench at Pune.
  • Trap: Special consideration for a gulf does not mean every location in that gulf has the same CRZ classification.

[Sources: MoEFCC, Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, 2019, paragraphs 3.1 and 10.1; MoEFCC, Annual Report 2025-26, Environmental Impact Assessment and Clearance, pp. 54-56, reporting period 1 January-31 December 2025; National Green Tribunal, RTI Manual updated 30 September 2025, Section 4(1)(b)(i), territorial jurisdiction of benches; NCERT, Class 8 Social and Political Life III, Chapter 10, Law and Social Justice; consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: One coastal development proposal connects ecological and livelihood concerns, which integrated management considers through regulation, safeguards and community involvement.
pictures.caption: Coastal management must consider environmental effects and community dependence together.

title: Coastal Regulation in Gujarat: Sensitive Gulfs, Development and Livelihoods

body:
Why a Specialised Environmental Tribunal Was Established

Environmental disputes may involve questions of law as well as scientific evidence. A case concerning polluted water, coastal construction or industrial emissions can require assessment of ecological effects, regulatory permissions and the rights of affected people.

The National Green Tribunal (NGT) was established to provide a specialised forum for the effective and expeditious disposal of qualifying environmental cases. It combines judicial expertise with environmental and scientific expertise.

Statutory Origin and Constitutional Background

The NGT was established under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, and began functioning on 18 October 2010. It is a statutory tribunal, not a constitutional court.

The Act was enacted on 2 June 2010. It provides for adjudication of specified environmental disputes and for relief, compensation and restoration where its jurisdictional requirements are met.

The broader constitutional background includes:

  • Article 21: Protection of life and personal liberty. Judicial interpretation has recognised a right to a healthy environment as part of the right to life.
  • Article 48A: A Directive Principle directing the State to endeavour to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife.
  • Article 51A(g): A Fundamental Duty of citizens to protect and improve the natural environment and have compassion for living creatures.

These constitutional provisions explain the importance of environmental protection. However, the NGT's specific jurisdiction and powers come from the NGT Act, not from Article 21 alone.

Composition of the Tribunal

The NGT has a full-time Chairperson, Judicial Members and Expert Members. The Act provides for 10 to 20 Judicial Members and 10 to 20 Expert Members, subject to the applicable statutory provisions.

The Chairperson must be, or have been, a Judge of the Supreme Court or Chief Justice of a High Court. Judicial Member eligibility includes High Court judges and advocates with 10 years' substantial environmental and forest litigation experience before the NGT, High Courts or Supreme Court. Expert Members bring the qualifications and experience specified for fields relevant to environmental protection and related scientific or technical matters.

The combination of legal and expert members is important because environmental cases often require decisions about both the meaning of a legal rule and the effects of an activity on the environment.

The Tribunal is guided by the principles of natural justice. This requires, among other things, giving parties an opportunity to present their cases and responding fairly to relevant evidence.

Principal and Zonal Benches

The NGT has a Principal Bench in New Delhi and zonal benches serving different parts of India.

ZonePlace of sittingImportant fact
NorthernNew DelhiPrincipal Bench
WesternPuneIncludes Gujarat
CentralBhopalServes the designated central region
SouthernChennaiServes the designated southern region
EasternKolkataServes the designated eastern region

These are the Tribunal's designated places of sitting. Actual hearing arrangements can also depend on administrative directions, staffing and the manner in which cases are assigned.

NGT and Other Environmental Institutions

The NGT has a different function from a Pollution Control Board or a Coastal Zone Management Authority. A pollution control body monitors and regulates pollution under its statutory powers. A Coastal Zone Management Authority performs its assigned coastal regulatory and clearance functions. The NGT decides qualifying legal disputes and specified statutory appeals.

Consequently, the NGT does not replace the authority that must grant CRZ clearance before a project begins.

Prelims focus

  • The National Green Tribunal Act was enacted on 2 June 2010.
  • The NGT was established with effect from 18 October 2010.
  • The NGT is a statutory tribunal with Judicial Members and Expert Members.
  • Its Principal Bench is in New Delhi.
  • The Western Zone Bench is at Pune and includes Gujarat.
  • Trap: The NGT decides environmental disputes; it is not the ordinary authority issuing CRZ permissions.

[Sources: National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, Sections 3-6 and 19; National Green Tribunal, RTI Manual updated 30 September 2025, organisation and territorial jurisdiction of benches; NCERT, Class 11 Indian Constitution at Work, Chapter 6, Judiciary; NCERT, Class 8 Social and Political Life III, Chapter 10, Law and Social Justice; consulted 1 November 2026.]

title: National Green Tribunal: Establishment, Composition and Benches

body:
Jurisdiction Means the Legal Power to Hear a Case

The NGT cannot decide every dispute merely because someone describes it as environmental. Its power depends on the type of claim, the statutory provision involved and, for appeals, the nature of the challenged order.

The NGT Act distinguishes among original environmental disputes, claims for compensation or restoration and appeals against specified decisions.

Section 14: Original Jurisdiction

Under Section 14, the Tribunal has jurisdiction over civil cases involving a substantial question relating to the environment, including enforcement of an environmental legal right, where the question arises from implementation of legislation specified in Schedule I.

A substantial environmental question may involve a significant breach of an environmental obligation, serious environmental consequences or wider public environmental concerns of the kind contemplated by the Act. A routine dispute with no qualifying environmental connection does not automatically come within this section.

The ordinary filing period for a Section 14 dispute is 6 months from when the cause of action first arose. The Tribunal may allow a further period of up to 60 days where sufficient cause prevented timely filing.

Section 15: Compensation and Restoration

Section 15 allows the Tribunal to order:

  • Relief and compensation for victims of pollution or other environmental damage arising under the scheduled enactments.
  • Restoration of damaged property.
  • Restoration of the affected environment.

For example, where qualifying industrial pollution damages a water body and nearby property, a remedy may address both the losses suffered by affected people and the measures needed to restore the environment. Paying compensation does not necessarily remove the responsibility to remedy environmental harm.

The ordinary limitation period for a Section 15 claim is 5 years from when the cause for relief or restoration first arose, with a possible further 60 days on sufficient cause.

Section 16: Appellate Jurisdiction

Section 16 permits appeals against specified orders and decisions made under the environmental laws identified in the section. These include particular environmental-clearance decisions under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, and other listed statutory decisions.

A person aggrieved by an appealable environmental-clearance decision may challenge its legality and compliance with applicable requirements. However, not every decision made by every government department is appealable to the NGT.

The normal appeal period is 30 days from communication of the decision, with a possible further 60 days if sufficient cause is established.

Section 22: Appeal from the NGT

An appeal against an NGT award, decision or order lies to the Supreme Court under Section 22. It must ordinarily be filed within 90 days of communication of the decision. The Supreme Court may entertain a later appeal if sufficient cause is shown.

The statutory appeal is confined to grounds of the kind specified in Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, principally a substantial question of law. It is not a routine opportunity to repeat every factual argument as though the case had never been heard.

Which Environmental Laws Are in Schedule I?

The original Schedule I to the NGT Act lists 7 enactments. Their identity is important because Section 14 expressly connects original jurisdiction to this Schedule.

Enactment listed in Schedule IYearCore subject
Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act1974Water pollution
Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Cess Act1977Historical water-pollution cess law; subsequently repealed
Forest (Conservation) Act1980Forest conservation; now titled Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam
Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act1981Air pollution
Environment (Protection) Act1986General environmental protection
Public Liability Insurance Act1991Relief associated with specified hazardous accidents
Biological Diversity Act2002Conservation and regulation of biological resources

The Water Cess Act, 1977, remains significant when studying the historical wording of Schedule I, but it was repealed through the legislative changes of 2017. A repealed statute should not be described as though it continues to levy the same cess.

The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 and Indian Forest Act, 1927 are not among the 7 enactments in the original Schedule I. A wildlife-related issue may still involve another scheduled environmental law, but the NGT's jurisdiction must be established through the statutory provisions actually invoked.

Section 18: Who Can Approach the NGT?

Depending on the type of proceeding, applicants may include affected individuals, property owners, legal representatives, persons aggrieved, representative bodies or organisations, governments, Pollution Control Boards and specified authorities.

This broader access recognises that environmental damage can affect a community or ecosystem even when no single individual owns the damaged resource. Nevertheless, the applicant must use the appropriate statutory procedure and satisfy the relevant requirements.

Prelims focus

  • Section 14: Substantial environmental disputes arising under Schedule I laws; 6 months plus a possible 60 days.
  • Section 15: Compensation and environmental or property restoration; 5 years plus a possible 60 days.
  • Section 16: Appeals against specified statutory orders; 30 days plus a possible 60 days.
  • Section 22: Appeal from the NGT to the Supreme Court; ordinarily within 90 days.
  • Schedule I originally lists 7 enactments, including the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
  • Trap: The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, is not itself listed in the original Schedule I.

[Sources: National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, Sections 14-18 and 22, and Schedule I; Government of India, Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2017, Section 18, and Lok Sabha Unstarred Question 2228, answered 28 July 2017, Annexure II; National Green Tribunal, official information on jurisdiction and applications; consulted 1 November 2026.]

title: NGT Jurisdiction, Scheduled Environmental Laws and Filing Periods

body:
Three Principles the NGT Must Apply

Section 20 of the National Green Tribunal Act requires the Tribunal to apply 3 important environmental principles when passing an order, decision or award. These principles are especially useful when evaluating industrial pollution, coastal development and damage to common natural resources.

1. Sustainable Development

Sustainable development seeks to meet present needs without undermining the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. In environmental decision-making, it requires attention to ecological limits alongside legitimate social and economic needs.

For example, improving coastal transport may be desirable, but a proposal should not destroy critical habitats when avoidable alternatives or protective measures are available. Sustainable development does not mean approving every project that promises employment, nor does it mean prohibiting all economic activity.

2. Precautionary Principle

The precautionary principle supports preventive action when a proposed activity creates a credible risk of serious environmental harm, even if every scientific detail is not yet certain.

The principle encourages authorities to examine potential damage before allowing an activity to proceed. A project should not be treated as harmless merely because complete scientific certainty about its future impacts is unavailable.

Suppose dredging near a sensitive coastal habitat presents a significant risk of damage. The decision-maker may require stronger assessment, safeguards or an alternative location rather than waiting until irreversible destruction has occurred.

3. Polluter Pays Principle

Under the polluter pays principle, those responsible for environmental pollution or damage should bear the appropriate costs of preventing, controlling and remedying that harm.

These costs may include compensation for affected people and measures needed for environmental restoration. The principle discourages shifting the cost of pollution onto surrounding communities or the public.

It does not mean that a person may lawfully pollute an area simply by offering to pay money afterward.

Sustainable development: Balance present development with long-term environmental protection.
Precautionary principle: Prevent serious environmental harm despite scientific uncertainty.
Polluter pays principle: Make the responsible polluter bear appropriate pollution and restoration costs.

Procedural Powers of the NGT

Section 19 provides that the NGT is not bound by the ordinary procedure prescribed by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, or by the evidence rules of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. Instead, it is guided by the principles of natural justice and may regulate its own procedure within the Act.

This procedural flexibility does not remove fairness or the requirement for relevant evidence. The Tribunal has important powers comparable to those exercised by civil courts for specified purposes, including summoning persons, requiring documents, receiving evidence and reviewing its decisions under the applicable law.

It may also grant interim orders and issue directions within its jurisdiction. Environmental cases sometimes require urgent action because continuing pollution or habitat destruction can make later remedies less effective.

What Remedies Can the NGT Provide?

Depending on the proceedings and applicable statutory provisions, the Tribunal may order or direct measures such as:

  • Stopping or restricting activities that violate environmental requirements.
  • Compliance with lawful pollution-control or environmental safeguards.
  • Compensation for qualifying environmental injury or damage.
  • Restoration of contaminated water, damaged land or affected ecosystems.
  • Other appropriate relief within its statutory powers.

Under Section 17, the Act also provides for no-fault liability in specified accident cases. This means liability may arise without requiring the affected person to prove negligence in the manner ordinarily required in a fault-based claim, subject to the statutory conditions.

Speed, Access and Enforcement

Section 18(3) states that the Tribunal should deal with applications and appeals as expeditiously as possible and endeavour to dispose of them finally within 6 months from filing, after giving the parties an opportunity to be heard.

The word endeavour matters. The provision expresses a statutory objective; it does not mean every NGT case is automatically decided within 6 months.

NGT decisions and directions are legally significant, and the Act contains provisions dealing with execution and penalties for non-compliance. Actual restoration, however, may require action by government departments, Pollution Control Boards, project operators and other implementing agencies.

Prelims focus

  • Section 20 expressly identifies sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle.
  • Section 19 makes natural justice central to NGT procedure.
  • The NGT is not bound by the ordinary procedural requirements of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
  • Section 15 authorises qualifying compensation and restoration remedies.
  • Section 18(3) sets an objective of disposing of cases within 6 months.
  • Trap: Polluter pays does not create a general right to pollute in exchange for payment.

[Sources: National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, Sections 15, 17-20 and 25-26; NCERT, Class 11 Indian Economic Development, Chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development; NCERT, Class 12 India: People and Economy, Chapter 12, Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems, discussion of pollution and environmental restoration; consulted 1 November 2026.]
title: NGT Environmental Principles, Remedies and Procedural Powers

body:
Two Different Parts of Environmental Governance

The Coastal Regulation Zone framework and the National Green Tribunal are closely connected, but they perform different functions.

CRZ regulation specifies where coastal activities may occur, what is prohibited and which permissions are necessary. It is primarily a framework for coastal planning, prior regulation and environmental safeguards.

The NGT is a statutory forum for deciding qualifying environmental disputes, hearing specified appeals and granting appropriate relief and restoration. It becomes relevant when a dispute falls within its legal jurisdiction.

FeatureCRZ frameworkNGT
Principal legal basisEnvironment (Protection) Act, 1986, and CRZ notificationsNational Green Tribunal Act, 2010
Main functionRegulate coastal land and water useAdjudicate qualifying environmental disputes
Key instrumentApproved CZMP and applicable notificationStatutory application, appeal and judicial order
Relevant authoritiesMoEFCC, CZMAs and other clearance authoritiesNGT Principal and zonal benches
Possible resultPermission, refusal or regulated conditionsDecision, directions, compensation or restoration

Worked Application: A Proposed Jetty Near a Gujarat Estuary

Consider a hypothetical proposal for a new jetty near a tidal estuary in Gujarat. Fishing boats already use the area, and mangroves occur along part of the bank.

Stage 1: Identify the Legal Coastal Area

The competent authority must establish the applicable approved CZMP and the precise HTL, LTL and CRZ classification. The jetty might involve intertidal land, tidal water or ecologically sensitive areas. These cannot be treated as one uniform category simply because they occur close together.

Stage 2: Examine Whether the Activity Is Permitted

A jetty is a foreshore-dependent activity that may be permitted under specified CRZ provisions. However, the proposal must still comply with restrictions affecting mangroves, reclamation, water quality and other environmental features.

Stage 3: Determine the Required Clearance

The responsible authority must identify whether the project attracts the EIA Notification, 2006, and which CRZ categories it occupies. Under the 2022 amendment, qualifying stand-alone jetties are among the specified projects handled by the concerned CZMA. A more extensive port development may require a different clearance route.

Stage 4: Consider Environmental and Livelihood Effects

Important questions include whether the project obstructs tidal flow, damages mangrove habitat, changes fishing access or produces pollution. Appropriate safeguards may involve design changes, protective conditions or refusal of an unsuitable proposal.

Stage 5: Understand When the NGT Becomes Relevant

If a qualifying substantial environmental dispute arises under a Schedule I law, or an appealable decision is challenged under Section 16, the NGT may have jurisdiction. It can examine relevant legal compliance and environmental harm within its powers. It does not simply take over the ordinary task of issuing a CRZ clearance.

Strengths of the NGT

  • Specialisation: Judicial and expert members can consider complex environmental evidence together.
  • Broader access: Specified individuals, organisations and authorities can approach the Tribunal under the Act.
  • Preventive and restorative approach: The Tribunal applies environmental principles and can order more than monetary compensation.
  • Dedicated environmental forum: Qualifying disputes and appeals are heard through a specialised statutory process.

Limitations and Practical Challenges

  • Limited statutory jurisdiction: The NGT cannot decide every dispute affecting nature. The claim or appeal must fall within the applicable provisions of the NGT Act.
  • Filing deadlines: Sections 14, 15 and 16 prescribe different limitation periods, restricting when proceedings may be initiated.
  • Implementation depends on other institutions: Environmental restoration and enforcement often require administrative action after an order.
  • Institutional capacity: Vacancies, workload, technical complexity and monitoring requirements can affect how quickly and effectively cases are resolved.
  • Development and livelihood conflicts: Protecting an ecosystem may require changes to projects or activities, while badly designed restrictions may burden people who depend on local resources. Decisions must address the legally relevant facts and competing interests.

Specialised environmental adjudication complements ordinary environmental administration. Neither one can replace effective planning, transparent mapping, lawful approvals or responsible enforcement.

One-Glance Conceptual Revision

The essential sequence is: identify the coastal area, apply the correct CRZ category, check the activity and clearance requirement, prevent or reduce environmental harm, and use the NGT when a qualifying dispute or appeal arises.

Prelims focus

  • CRZ classification depends on the officially approved coastal map and applicable notification.
  • The legal treatment of a project depends on its location, activity and any applicable exceptions.
  • CZMAs and clearance authorities regulate coastal projects; the NGT adjudicates qualifying disputes and appeals.
  • For Gujarat, the designated NGT zonal bench is at Pune.
  • The NGT must apply sustainable development, precaution and polluter pays under Section 20.
  • Trap: Environmental importance alone does not establish NGT jurisdiction; the relevant statutory conditions must also be satisfied.

[Sources: MoEFCC, Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, 2019, paragraphs 2-8; MoEFCC, S.O. 5495(E), dated 24 November 2022; National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, Sections 14-20 and 22; National Green Tribunal, RTI Manual updated 30 September 2025; NCERT, Class 8 Social and Political Life III, Chapter 10, Law and Social Justice; consulted 1 November 2026.]
